---
title: Language Server Development
description: >
  How the Panache language server works: incremental document synchronization,
  parsing, and the LSP features it implements.
---

### Document Synchronization

The language server tracks document changes using **incremental
synchronization**:

`textDocument/didOpen`
:   The editor opens a document.

`textDocument/didChange`
:   The editor sends incremental changes to the document's content.

`textDocument/didClose`
:   The editor closes a document.

These notifications keep the server's document state current while minimizing
data transfer.

### One Tree, Derived on Demand

Notification handlers write Salsa *inputs* without parsing. All consumers,
including request handlers, the linter, and diagnostics, read the tree from the
`parsed_document` query. Each document therefore has exactly one parse per
revision, and handlers always see a tree that matches the text they receive.

Quarto diagnostics load the embedded validation schema once, on first use. The
schema decoder constructs nested nodes directly to avoid buffering temporary
subtrees during the first analysis. The `benches/lsp_first_open.py` benchmark
measures that shared initialization cost separately from each document's
analysis time.

### One Line Index for Updates and Requests

A `LineIndex` (`src/lsp/line_index.rs`) converts document positions. It stores
line start offsets and a flag for each line indicating whether it contains any
non-ASCII bytes. Each conversion uses a binary search. On all-ASCII lines, which
account for nearly all lines, the remaining work is plain arithmetic.

A `LineIndexCache` stores one index per open document. The writer and every
worker snapshot share a handle to this cache. `did_change` takes the index out,
patches it with `replace_range`, and puts it back. The patch shifts the line
table rather than rescanning the document. Request handlers retrieve the same
entry, so updates and requests use the index produced by the last keystroke.

The index is cached outside Salsa because each keystroke updates the text input,
invalidating any memo keyed on it. When the index was a Salsa query, every
request the editor issued between keystrokes rebuilt the index over the whole
document, even though the writer already held an index for those bytes. There
were also two live `Arc`s to the index, which turned the writer's in-place patch
into a table copy.

Sharing is safe because **the cache checks every entry before returning it**. It
returns an entry only if the entry shares the text allocation Salsa holds, as
checked by `Arc::ptr_eq`. An `Arc<str>` is immutable, and an edit replaces the
handle rather than writing through it. A shared allocation therefore proves that
the index describes the current bytes without reading them.

Any other update to the text, whether from a watcher event, disk
resynchronization, or reopening the document, invalidates the entry without
requiring the writer to know about the cache. A reader with an invalid entry
must rebuild the index and cannot return an answer based on stale bytes. The
cache requires allocation identity, whereas the reparse base described below
also accepts equal contents. A stale base only widens the next diff, but a stale
line index would produce a wrong answer.

### Incremental Parsing

By default, `parsed_document` reuses the previous parse by splicing in changes
rather than reparsing from scratch. Set `PANACHE_INCREMENTAL_PARSING=0` to turn
this off for debugging. The deprecated `experimental.incrementalParsing = false`
client setting also disables it. The previous parse lives in a side channel
alongside Salsa (`src/incremental.rs`), keyed on `(file, config)`. It is reused
only when both the config value and the document's reference-definition set are
unchanged. Retained blocks keep the reference resolution and options from their
original parse, so a change to either can invalidate blocks far from the edit.

The query attempts a splice in four tiers, cheapest first, and uses the first
one that succeeds:

- **Token.** An edit strictly inside one plain-prose `TEXT` token of a top-level
  paragraph replaces that green token. Its cost depends on the token's length
  plus a green root rebuild. Like the region tier below, this work does not
  scale with document size. For an accepted edit, a keystroke in a 300 KB file
  therefore costs the same as a keystroke in a small file. The token tier runs
  before the cost guards described below, so a successful splice also avoids the
  cost of evaluating them. Its guards are strict: the edit must not touch either
  end of the token's non-whitespace core, every byte of the token must be inert
  prose, the token must still parse as a single `TEXT` token in isolation, and
  the edit must fall after the first word on its line so it cannot create a
  block marker.
- **Region.** Reparses one contiguous run of top-level `DOCUMENT` children. The
  run covers the edit and extends until a blank line sits on each side. The
  parse is *bounded*: it covers only the region, so an edit near the top of a
  large file costs the same as an edit near the bottom. It handles most edits in
  ordinary prose documents.
- **Section window.** Reparses from the previous top-level heading and reuses
  the old tail, preserving its `Arc` identity, when the reparsed tail is
  structurally equal.
- **Suffix window.** Reparses from the enclosing block.

The two window tiers parse to the end of the document. The region tier parses a
bounded fragment and checks its boundaries against neighboring blocks. A
fragment parsed in isolation is unreliable because list-item buffering, fence
pairing, and table detection depend on lookahead beyond its end. To check each
seam, the parser reparses the fragment together with the neighboring block on
that side. The check succeeds only if no top-level child straddles the seam, the
fragment produces exactly the same children and errors as it did in isolation,
and the neighbor remains byte-identical. An open construct, such as an unclosed
fence or div, consumes following content greedily and therefore reaches the
neighboring block, where the check catches it.

Two constructs can reach beyond one neighbor and escape any boundary parse. A
fence can pair with an opener several blocks back. Under the Pandoc dialect, an
*unclosed* fence is ordinary paragraph text, so the opener looks inert. A
multiline-table border can pair across arbitrarily many blank-line-separated
blocks. The region tier guards against both cases by comparing the region's
delimiter lines before and after the edit. If they are unchanged, the document's
entire sequence of delimiter lines is unchanged, so no pairing can move. This
permits edits to prose, a table cell, or a code block's body, and rejects edits
that add, remove, or alter a delimiter.

All four tiers remain because all four are used. Across the fuzzer's corpus of
real documents, the region tier handles about three quarters of splices, the
section window a seventh, and the suffix window and token tier the rest. On
documents without headings, the suffix window becomes the workhorse instead.
`crates/panache-parser/tests/incremental_fuzz.rs` prints this histogram on every
run.

Four properties make the side channel safe to read and write from an otherwise
pure query:

- A successful splice is byte-identical to a full parse, including both the tree
  and syntax errors. The parser asserts this on every splice in debug builds.
  Setting `PANACHE_REPARSE_ORACLE=1` adds a second check against a full parse
  before anything is stored. Each oracle costs a full parse, so both are
  compiled out of release builds. Every build still checks one `O(1)` invariant:
  the spliced tree spans exactly the text it was spliced from. If this check
  fails, the query falls back to a full parse rather than panicking. This
  matters because `parsed_document` feeds the formatter, which writes the user's
  file.

- Every guard returns `None` when it cannot accept a splice, so the query falls
  back to an ordinary full parse.

- Two guards reject splices on cost grounds. Both *window* strategies parse
  their window to the end of the document. A window starting near the top of the
  file reparses nearly all of it and adds the cost of a splice. Measurements
  show a 5-10% loss compared with a full parse, so the guard rejects windows
  that cover more than 85% of the document.

  The *region* tier performs a fragment parse and up to two boundary parses,
  each including a neighbor, amounting to roughly three region-sized parses. For
  the same reason, its guard rejects a region that covers more than a quarter of
  the document, counting its neighbors as well as itself. Both guards run before
  any parse. A whole-document replacement, which some clients send on every
  format-on-save, fails both guards and incurs only the full parse it would have
  needed anyway. `benches/lsp_incremental.rs` contains the measurements and a
  case on each side of both thresholds.

- The base is stored last, after every fallible step, so a panic or a Salsa
  cancellation during the query cannot leave a base whose text and tree
  disagree. Stores are not ordered across revisions, so an older base can
  overwrite a newer one. Each is internally consistent, and a stale base only
  widens the next diff.

Only the language server adds documents to the side channel, and only while
incremental parsing is enabled. It is enabled by default unless a client or
`PANACHE_INCREMENTAL_PARSING=0` disables it. When it is disabled, no documents
are added, so every parse is a full parse.

### Durability and Invalidation Policy

Panache uses Salsa durability levels to reduce unnecessary revalidation in LSP
mode.

#### Durability assignments

`LOW`
:   Updates to the active document's open-buffer text (`didOpen`, `didChange`).

`MEDIUM`
:   Per-document config updates and file-watcher refreshes for dependency files
    already in the cache.

`HIGH`
:   Dependency files loaded from disk and cached from the project graph.

#### Invalidation policy

- Edits while typing should invalidate low-durability data aggressively without
  forcing broad revalidation of stable dependency data.
- Config reloads and watcher events use medium durability so changes propagate
  with less churn than open-buffer edits.
- Disk-cached dependencies use high durability so unrelated low-frequency edits
  do not repeatedly revalidate those inputs.

#### Verification and measurement

The durability revalidation measurement harness is `tests/durability_bench.rs`.
It is ignored by default. Run it with:

```bash
cargo test --test durability_bench durability_revalidation_bench -- --ignored --nocapture
```

Policy regression tests in `src/salsa.rs` verify that stable high-durability
inputs avoid revalidation under low-durability updates, while stable
low-durability inputs are revalidated.
